module_title: Safe Use of Pesticides and Chemicals

lessons.title: Types of Pesticides: Insecticides, Rodenticides, and Fumigants
lessons.body:
Pesticides are chemicals used to kill or control pests. In pest control, you will mainly work with three types: insecticides, rodenticides, and fumigants. Insecticides target insects like cockroaches, mosquitoes, and termites. Common active ingredients include permethrin, deltamethrin, and cypermethrin. These are often sold as concentrates that you mix with water. For example, a 10% cypermethrin concentrate might be mixed at 5ml per litre of water for spraying. Rodenticides kill rodents like rats and mice. The most common are anticoagulants such as brodifacoum and bromadiolone. They come as baitsâblocks, pellets, or tracking powder. A single 20g block of brodifacoum bait can kill a rat after it feeds for a few days. Fumigants are gases that kill pests in enclosed spaces. Examples are aluminium phosphide (which releases phosphine gas) and methyl bromide. Fumigants are extremely dangerous and require special training and licences. In many African countries, only certified operators can use them. For a small pest control business, you will likely start with insecticides and rodenticides, and hire a licensed fumigator for termite or bedbug jobs that need fumigation.

Always check the label to know which type you are using. Insecticides may be contact killers (kill on touch) or stomach poisons (insects eat them). Rodenticides are mostly stomach poisons. Fumigants are inhaled. Never mix different types unless the label says you can. Mixing an insecticide with a rodenticide is useless and dangerous. Store each type separately in locked cabinets. Keep a log of what you buy and use. In Africa, fake or expired pesticides are common in open markets. Buy only from registered agro-dealers and check the expiry date. If a deal seems too cheap, it is likely fake. Using fake chemicals wastes money and can harm you, your clients, and the environment.

lessons.title: Reading and Understanding Pesticide Labels and Safety Data Sheets
lessons.body:
Every pesticide container must have a label. The label is your legal and safety guide. Before you open any container, read the label from top to bottom. Key sections include: product name, active ingredient and concentration (e.g., 20% w/v cypermethrin), target pests, mixing instructions, application rate, safety precautions, first aid, and storage. The label also has a colour band: green (slightly toxic), yellow (moderately toxic), blue (highly toxic), and red (extremely toxic). In many African countries, red-band products are restricted. For example, a red-band product like aluminium phosphide requires a licence. Never use a product without a label. If the label is torn or missing, return it to the seller.

Safety Data Sheets (SDS) give more detailed information. They have 16 sections, including: identification, hazards, first aid, firefighting, accidental release, handling and storage, exposure controls, physical properties, stability, toxicology, ecology, disposal, transport, and regulatory information. As a business, you must keep an SDS for every chemical you use, either printed or on your phone. If a client or inspector asks, you must show it. The SDS tells you what PPE to wear, what to do if you spill, and how to treat exposure. For example, an SDS for a pyrethroid insecticide might say: wear nitrile gloves, goggles, and a respirator; if swallowed, do not induce vomiting, seek medical help. The label gives quick facts; the SDS gives details. Always follow both. In Africa, where internet may be limited, download SDSs when you have network and save them offline. Teach your workers to read labels in their own language if possible. Many manufacturers provide labels in English, French, and Portuguese. If your worker cannot read, train them using pictures and symbols. Never assume you know what a product doesâread the label every time, even for products you have used before.

lessons.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) for Pest Control Operators
lessons.body:
PPE is your last line of defence against pesticide poisoning. You must wear the right PPE for every task. The minimum for mixing and spraying liquid insecticides: nitrile gloves (not latexâlatex does not resist many solvents), chemical-resistant coveralls or long-sleeved shirt and trousers, rubber boots, goggles or face shield, and a respirator with a P2 or P3 filter. For fumigation, you need a full-face respirator with a specific canister (e.g., for phosphine, use a canister rated for inorganic gases) and a gas monitor. Never wear cotton glovesâthey absorb chemicals. Never wear shorts or sandals. In hot African climates, you may be tempted to remove PPE, but heat stroke is less likely than poisoning if you take breaks. Work in early morning or late afternoon to avoid extreme heat.

How to put on and remove PPE: Put on in a clean area, away from chemicals. Start with coveralls, then boots, then respirator, then goggles, then gloves last. When removing, do it in reverse: gloves first, then goggles, respirator, boots, coveralls. Wash reusable PPE with soap and water after each use. Store in a clean, dry place. Inspect before each use: check gloves for holes (fill with water and squeeze), check respirator filters for expiry, check goggles for cracks. Replace filters according to manufacturer instructions or when breathing becomes difficult. For rodenticide baiting, you need gloves and coveralls, but a respirator is not usually needed unless the bait is dusty. For fumigation, you also need a personal gas monitor and a buddy systemânever work alone. In Africa, buy PPE from safety supply shops or online. A good nitrile glove costs about $1 per pair; a half-face respirator with cartridges costs $30â$50. This is a small price compared to hospital bills. Train your workers on PPE use and keep records. Make PPE a condition of employment.

lessons.title: Safe Mixing, Application, and Storage of Pesticides
lessons.body:
Mixing is the most dangerous step because you handle concentrated chemicals. Always mix outdoors or in a well-ventilated area, never in a kitchen or enclosed room. Use a dedicated mixing station: a table with a lip to contain spills, a water source, and a bucket for rinsing. Wear full PPE. Read the label for the correct mixing ratio. For example, if the label says 10ml per 10 litres of water, use a measuring cupânever guess. Use the 'triple rinse' method for empty containers: fill the container one-third with water, shake for 30 seconds, pour into the spray tank, repeat three times. Add the rinse water to the tank. This gets all chemical out and prevents waste. Never mix different pesticides unless the label says it is safe. Mix only what you need for the day. Leftover mix cannot be storedâit may degrade or become more toxic. Spray it on a labelled area or dispose of it as hazardous waste.

Application: Choose the right equipment. For spraying, use a knapsack sprayer with a pressure gauge and correct nozzle. Calibrate before each job: spray water on a measured area (e.g., 10m x 10m) and measure how much water you use. Adjust walking speed or nozzle to get the correct dose. For rodenticides, place bait in tamper-resistant bait stations. Secure them so children and pets cannot access. For fumigation, seal the area with gas-proof sheets and post warning signs. Never apply pesticides near food, water sources, or where children play. After application, wash hands and face, remove PPE, and shower. Storage: Keep pesticides in a locked, ventilated cabinet, away from food, feed, and water. Store in original containers with labels intact. Keep a log of inventory: date, product, quantity, and who used it. In Africa, heat and humidity can degrade chemicals. Store in a cool, dry place. Never store pesticides in soda bottles or unlabelled containersâthis causes accidental poisoning. Dispose of expired chemicals through a licensed waste handler.

lessons.title: First Aid for Pesticide Exposure and Poisoning
lessons.body:
Pesticide poisoning can happen through skin contact, inhalation, or swallowing. Know the signs: skin contact causes redness, itching, or burns; inhalation causes coughing, dizziness, headache, or difficulty breathing; swallowing causes nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or convulsions. If someone shows these signs, act fast. First, protect yourselfâput on gloves and a respirator before helping. Move the person to fresh air immediately. If the pesticide is on the skin, remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin with plenty of soap and water for at least 15 minutes. Do not scrub hard. If in the eyes, flush with clean water for 15â20 minutes, holding eyelids open. If swallowed, do not induce vomiting unless the label says to. For many pesticides, inducing vomiting can cause more damage. Check the label and SDS for specific first aid instructions. For example, if a pyrethroid is swallowed, give activated charcoal if available and the person is conscious. Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious person.

Call for medical help immediately. In Africa, have emergency numbers saved: local poison control centre, nearest hospital, and a trusted doctor. If you are far from a hospital, call for advice while transporting. Bring the pesticide container or label to the hospitalâthis helps doctors choose the right treatment. For organophosphate poisoning, an antidote (atropine) may be needed. For anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, vitamin K1 is the antidote. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen. After first aid, report the incident to your supervisor and write an incident report. Investigate what went wrong and improve your safety procedures. Keep a first aid kit in your vehicle and at your mixing station. It should include: soap, clean water, eye wash, activated charcoal, bandages, and a list of emergency numbers. Train all workers in first aid. In many African countries, basic first aid training is available through the Red Cross. Make it a requirement for your team.

lessons.title: Disposal of Empty Pesticide Containers and Waste
lessons.body:
Empty pesticide containers are hazardous waste. Never reuse them for drinking water, food, or animal feed. Never burn themâburning releases toxic fumes. Never throw them in rivers or open dumps. The correct method: triple rinse the container as soon as it is empty. Then puncture or crush it so it cannot be reused. Store rinsed containers in a secure area until you can take them to a licensed hazardous waste disposal facility. In many African countries, local councils or agro-dealers have collection points for empty containers. If none exists, contact the manufacturer or a registered waste handler. For small amounts, you can bury them in a lined pit away from water sources, but only if local regulations allow. Check with your environmental authority. For unused or expired pesticides, never pour them down the drain or on the ground. Take them to a hazardous waste facility. Some countries have 'pesticide take-back' programmes. If not, store them safely until a disposal option is available.

Other waste: contaminated PPE, spill cleanup materials, and leftover spray mix are also hazardous. Place them in sealed bags or drums. Label them 'Hazardous WasteâPesticide'. Do not mix with regular garbage. For spill cleanup: use absorbent material like sawdust or sand, sweep it up, and place in a sealed container. Wash the area with soap and water. Never hose down a spill into a drain. As a business, keep a waste disposal log: date, type of waste, quantity, and disposal method. This shows you are responsible and helps if inspectors visit. In Africa, illegal dumping of pesticide containers is common. Be a leaderâoffer to collect empty containers from your clients for safe disposal, and charge a small fee. This adds value to your service and protects the community. Remember, proper disposal is not just legalâit prevents poisoning of children, animals, and water sources. Make it part of your standard operating procedure.

quiz.q: Which type of pesticide is designed to kill rodents?
quiz.explanation: Rodenticides are specifically formulated to kill rodents like rats and mice.

quiz.q: What is the most common active ingredient in anticoagulant rodenticides?
quiz.explanation: Brodifacoum is a common anticoagulant rodenticide that causes fatal bleeding.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fumigant?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium phosphide releases phosphine gas, which is a fumigant.

quiz.q: Why should you never mix an insecticide with a rodenticide?
options: A) It makes the mixture more toxic
B) It is useless and dangerous
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Mixing different pesticide types is ineffective and can create unpredictable hazards.

quiz.q: What colour band on a pesticide label indicates 'extremely toxic'?
quiz.explanation: Red band indicates extremely toxic products, often restricted.

quiz.q: What information is found on a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) but not usually on a label?
quiz.explanation: SDS includes detailed toxicological information, while labels give basic first aid.

quiz.q: How many sections does a standard Safety Data Sheet have?
quiz.explanation: SDSs are standardized with 16 sections covering all safety aspects.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pesticide label is torn or missing?
options: B) Return it to the seller
quiz.explanation: Without a label, you cannot safely use the product; return it to the seller.

quiz.q: Which glove material is recommended for handling pesticides?
quiz.explanation: Nitrile gloves resist many solvents and chemicals better than latex or cotton.

quiz.q: What type of respirator filter is needed for most liquid insecticide spraying?
quiz.explanation: P2 or P3 filters capture fine particles and aerosols from spraying.

quiz.q: When removing PPE, which item should be removed first?
quiz.explanation: Gloves are removed first to avoid contaminating other PPE or skin.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect reusable PPE?
options: D) Only when it looks dirty
quiz.explanation: PPE should be inspected before each use to ensure it is not damaged.

quiz.q: What is the 'triple rinse' method used for?
quiz.explanation: Triple rinsing removes residual pesticide from empty containers for safe disposal.

quiz.q: Why should you never store leftover mixed pesticide spray?
options: B) It may degrade or become more toxic
quiz.explanation: Leftover mix can degrade or become more toxic; it should be used or disposed of immediately.

quiz.q: Where should pesticides be stored?
options: B) In a locked, ventilated cabinet away from food
quiz.explanation: Pesticides must be stored in a locked, ventilated area away from food, feed, and water.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if someone gets pesticide in their eyes?
options: B) Flush with clean water for 15â20 minutes
quiz.explanation: Flushing with water for 15â20 minutes is the immediate first aid for eye exposure.

quiz.q: If a person swallows a pesticide, what should you NOT do?
options: B) Induce vomiting unless the label says to
C) Give activated charcoal if conscious
D) Bring the container to the hospital
quiz.explanation: Inducing vomiting can cause more damage; follow label instructions.

quiz.q: Which antidote is used for anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin K1 is the specific antidote for anticoagulant rodenticides.

quiz.q: What should you bring to the hospital when a poisoning occurs?
options: A) The pesticide container or label
quiz.explanation: The container or label helps doctors identify the chemical and choose treatment.

quiz.q: How should you dispose of empty pesticide containers?
options: C) Triple rinse, puncture, and take to a hazardous waste facility
quiz.explanation: Triple rinsing, puncturing, and proper hazardous waste disposal prevent poisoning.

quiz.q: Why should you never burn empty pesticide containers?
options: D) It is not allowed by manufacturers
quiz.explanation: Burning pesticide containers releases toxic fumes that harm health and environment.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to clean up a pesticide spill?
options: A) Hose it into a drain
B) Use absorbent material, sweep, and seal in a container
quiz.explanation: Absorbents like sawdust or sand should be used, then sealed for hazardous waste.

quiz.q: What does a green colour band on a pesticide label indicate?
quiz.explanation: Green band indicates slightly toxic or low hazard products.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended practice when mixing pesticides?
options: D) Mix in an enclosed kitchen
quiz.explanation: Mixing should never be done in an enclosed space due to inhalation risk.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of calibrating a sprayer?
options: B) To ensure correct dose of pesticide per area
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures you apply the correct amount of pesticide over a given area.

quiz.q: Where should bait stations be placed?
options: B) In tamper-resistant stations secure from children and pets
quiz.explanation: Tamper-resistant bait stations protect children, pets, and non-target animals.

quiz.q: What should be included in a first aid kit for pesticide exposure?
options: A) Soap, clean water, eye wash, activated charcoal
quiz.explanation: Soap, water, eye wash, and activated charcoal are essential for pesticide first aid.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a waste disposal log?
options: A) To show responsibility and comply with regulations
quiz.explanation: A waste log demonstrates responsible disposal and helps during inspections.

quiz.q: What should you do with expired pesticides?
options: C) Take to a hazardous waste facility
quiz.explanation: Expired pesticides must be disposed of through licensed hazardous waste facilities.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of pesticide poisoning by inhalation?
quiz.explanation: Inhalation of pesticides commonly causes coughing, dizziness, and breathing difficulty.
